scenes.visual: Dark slate background with slow drifting particles, reusing the first film's colour map (teal animal receptors, amber bacterial sensor/diverged receptors, gold phosphates, coral core kinases, violet reader domains). Clean white title card centered: 'Why Animal Pathways Rewire Cheaply'.

scenes.tts: In the first film, duplication multiplied animal receptors over a shared core. How does a copied receptor plug into a new pathway without inventing a new enzyme? Start with a simpler design.

scenes.tts: Many bacteria use a two component relay. A membrane sensor kinase takes one phosphate from A T P and puts it on its own histidine. Its partner responder moves that phosphate onto its own aspartate, flipping its shape to switch genes on. The sensor's enzyme has a different fold from animal kinases, and animals lack this system.
scenes.caption: Many bacteria use a two-component relay. A membrane sensor kinase takes one phosphate from ATP and puts it on its own histidine. scenes.visual: Schematic of a bacterial membrane filling 65 percent of frame height. An amber block ('Sensor kinase') grabs a gold phosphate dot from an ATP icon onto a notch labelled 'His'. A single partner block ('Responder') docks, transfers the gold dot onto 'Asp', visibly bends its shape, and activates a DNA switch. A neat caption notes 'Different fold; absent in animals'.

scenes.tts: Notice that mark. A phosphate on aspartate is short lived. The responder itself helps shed it, within seconds for some, minutes or more for others. It changes only that responder. On an animal receptor tail, a phosphate on tyrosine stays until a phosphatase removes it. What new kind of connection does a lasting mark allow?

scenes.visual: Hold the split schematic on screen—flickering gold 'Asp' phosphate on the left, steady glowing gold 'Tyr' phosphate on the right—with slow ambient drift. A high-contrast question card pulses gently at center bottom: 'What new kind of connection does a lasting mark allow?'

scenes.tts: Because the mark stays put, it acts as a docking tag. Separate reader pieces, like S H 2 domains, bind the marked tyrosine and recruit downstream pathways. One receptor can hold several marks and launch several branches at once.
scenes.caption: Because the mark stays put, it acts as a docking tag. Separate reader pieces, like SH2 domains, bind the marked tyrosine and recruit downstream pathways. One receptor can hold several marks and launch several branches at once.
scenes.visual: The animal teal receptor expands to center stage. Two steady gold phosphates glow on its tail. Violet block modules labelled 'SH2 reader' drift in from the cytoplasm and click onto each gold mark, pulling two coral downstream kinase branches into motion at once.
scenes.narration: Because the mark stays put, it acts as a docking tag. Separate reader pieces, like SH2 domains, bind the marked tyrosine and recruit downstream pathways. One receptor can hold several marks and launch several branches at once.

scenes.tts: Modular parts make rewiring cheap in three ways. A domain is a folded piece of protein that works on its own. First, moving an S H 2 domain onto another protein builds a new link in one step. Second, mutating one or two amino acids beside a tyrosine builds a new docking site.

scenes.visual: Schematic stays on the teal receptor and cytoplasm. Move 1: a violet 'SH2' block detaches and snaps cleanly onto a new coral effector block, which then docks on the receptor tail. Move 2: zoom onto a tail 'Tyr' with two grey neighbour beads; one bead flips to violet, creating a shaped slot labelled 'New docking site' that catches a different violet SH2 adaptor.

scenes.tts: Third, regulatory D N A is a short stretch, usually near a gene, that decides which cells build it. Changing it puts an unchanged receptor into a new tissue with different targets. Genome counts match: budding yeast has one S H 2 protein, while humans carry over a hundred.

scenes.visual: Move 3 schematic: a short violet DNA switch beside a receptor gene changes colour, and the exact same teal receptor appears in a second cell outline filled with different coral target blocks. Beside it, a clean counter compares 'Yeast: 1 SH2' with 'Human: >100 SH2'.

scenes.tts: When did this tyrosine toolkit appear? Look at a choanoflagellate, the closest living single celled relative of animals. It carries one hundred twenty eight tyrosine kinases to our ninety, plus tyrosine phosphatases and S H 2 domains. Yet it lacks recognisable genes for pathways like T G F beta. Parts shared by animals and their closest relative were likely in their common ancestor, so the kit predates animals. Its job in one cell is largely unknown.

scenes.visual: Schematic cartoon of a collared, single-celled choanoflagellate (labelled 'Monosiga brevicollis') beside a human cell outline, under the label 'Closest living single-celled relative of animals'. Computed count bars grow as spoken: 'Human: 90 TKs' vs. 'Monosiga: 128 TKs'. Inside Monosiga, three icons light up—teal 'Writer (TK)', violet 'Reader (SH2)', coral 'Eraser (PTP)'—beside an empty outline labelled 'No TGF-beta / Wnt' and a gentle '?' labelled 'Single-cell role largely unknown'.

scenes.tts: Rewiring copied receptors into shared hubs builds a network rather than separate wires. If one receptor fails, sisters made in the same cells can cover part of the loss. Hubs buy robustness, but they bring clinical costs too. Modular domains, short motifs, and regulatory D N A make new wiring cheap.

scenes.visual: Return to the carried multi-receptor membrane over the coral hub. One teal receptor dims as if blocked, and signal pulses reroute through an amber sister receptor in the same cell into the same coral hub, keeping the downstream output bar steady. Subtle labels highlight the three modular tools—'Domains', 'Short motifs', 'Regulatory DNA'—converging around the network.
